questions.question: In C++, what occurs when a program attempts to write to an array index beyond its declared bounds, such as `day[5] = 75;` for `int day[5];`?
options: The operating system automatically doubles the array's capacity
The program intercepts the access and routes the value to index 0
The compiler flags a syntax error and prevents executable creation
C++ performs no bounds checking; it compiles cleanly but risks memory corruption, unexpected values, or runtime crashes
questions.explanation: In C++, exceeding array index bounds is not a compilation or syntax error because no bounds checking is performed; it causes logical errors or runtime faults.

questions.question: Given `char mystring[] = "Hello";`, why does the assignment statement `mystring = "World";` fail to compile in C++?
options: "World" has fewer characters than "Hello"
String assignments in C++ require single quotation marks
The assignment operator can only be used on string class objects, never pointers
An array identifier is a constant pointer to its allocated memory block, and constant identifiers cannot be assigned new values
questions.explanation: An array name is a constant pointer to the first element; because it is constant, assigning a new address or string literal to it after definition is illegal.

questions.question: Inside a function where a local variable `int num1 = 33;` shadows a global variable `int num1 = 2;`, which statement correctly outputs the global variable?
options: cout << extern(num1);
cout << ::num1;
cout << num1::global;
cout << global.num1;
questions.explanation: The unary scope resolution operator (::) with no preceding class or namespace name accesses the variable defined at global scope.

questions.question: Under which condition will a C++ compiler typically refuse to inline a function even if declared with the `inline` keyword?
options: The function is called multiple times within main()
The function calls itself recursively or contains loops such as for or while
The function accepts more than two parameters
The function return type is a fundamental type such as int or float
questions.explanation: Compilers treat inline as a suggestion and will decline to inline functions that are recursive, contain loops, or are too large in code size.

questions.question: What is the operational difference between executing `var1 = *p1++;` and `var2 = *++p2;`?
options: Both statements produce identical results because ++ and * have identical precedence
*p1++ is invalid C++ syntax, whereas *++p2 is valid
*p1++ increments the value in memory, while *++p2 increments the pointer address
*p1++ dereferences the original pointer before incrementing it, while *++p2 increments the pointer first and then dereferences the new address
questions.explanation: Post-increment has higher precedence but yields the original pointer for dereference before incrementing. Pre-increment increments the pointer first before dereferencing.

questions.question: Consider the code: `int *p1 = new int; int *p2 = new int; *p1 = 10; *p2 = 20; p1 = p2; *p1 = 30;`. What values are printed by `cout << *p1 << " " << *p2;`?
questions.explanation: After pointer assignment p1 = p2, both p1 and p2 point to the exact same dynamic integer. Changing *p1 to 30 modifies that shared location, so both print 30.

questions.question: How does data storage fundamentally differ between text files and binary files in C++?
options: Text files write out data as formatted ASCII character sequences, while binary files write raw data in the exact representation used in main memory
Text files can only be accessed using seekg(), while binary files only support sequential reading
Binary files are universally portable across all operating systems, while text files are machine-dependent
Binary files format numbers with commas and newlines, while text files use raw bit streams
questions.explanation: Text files store numbers converted into sequences of ASCII characters, whereas binary files store data compactly in the identical binary format used in RAM.

questions.question: In a program reading a file backwards character by character, after reading one character forward with `indata >> inchar;`, how should `seekg()` be invoked to move to the preceding character?
options: indata.seekg(-1L, ios::cur);
indata.seekg(-1L, ios::beg);
indata.seekg(-2L, ios::cur);
indata.seekg(0L, ios::beg);
questions.explanation: Because reading the character advanced the stream pointer forward by 1 byte, the program must seek backward by 2 bytes relative to the current position (ios::cur) to reach the preceding byte.

questions.question: Given the statement `YourClass yetAnotherObject();`, how does the C++ compiler actually interpret this declaration?
options: As a function prototype declaration for a function named yetAnotherObject returning a YourClass object
As a syntax error because empty parentheses are disallowed in C++
As an object instantiation calling the default constructor
As an array declaration of zero elements
questions.explanation: In C++, declaring an object with empty parentheses is parsed as a function declaration that takes no arguments and returns an object of type YourClass.

questions.question: At what point is memory actually allocated for class data members in C++?
options: When an object instance of the class is created/instantiated
During the preprocessing phase
When the class definition is compiled
When member function prototypes are declared
questions.explanation: Defining a class creates a user-defined blueprint without allocating memory; storage for data members is allocated only when an object of the class is instantiated.

questions.question: In physical memory, how does C++ store a two-dimensional array declared as `int matrix[3][5]`?
options: As a binary search tree of integers
As a single contiguous sequence of 15 integers arranged in row-major order
As 5 vertical column vectors stored separately in the heap
As three non-contiguous arrays linked together through pointer tables
questions.explanation: Multidimensional arrays in C++ are an abstraction stored in contiguous memory in row-major order, equivalent to a flat array of 15 elements (3 * 5 = 15).

questions.question: Given `int a = 1; int day[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50}; day[a] = 5;`, what occurs when evaluating the expression `day[day[a]]`?
options: It returns day[0] which equals 10
It accesses day[5], which exceeds the valid array bounds [0, 4]
It returns day[1] which equals 20
It causes a compilation syntax error during index evaluation
questions.explanation: Since day[a] (day[1]) is assigned 5, the expression day[day[a]] evaluates to day[5], which is out of bounds for an array of size 5.

questions.question: Why does recursion generally involve higher memory consumption and processor overhead than an equivalent iterative loop?
options: Each recursive call creates an activation record (stack frame) on the runtime stack storing parameters and local variables
Iteration requires allocating memory on the heap, whereas recursion does not
Recursion prevents the compiler from optimizing variable names
Recursive functions are executed in an external virtual machine
questions.explanation: Each recursive call pushes a stack frame with its local variables and parameters onto the runtime stack, incurring processor call overhead and substantial memory use.

questions.question: Given `void Mult_Display(int x, char y);`, why is the function call `Mult_Display('A', 5);` valid and executable in C++?
options: Single quotes and numeric literals are considered identical types in C++
The compiler creates a duplicate overloaded function at runtime
The compiler strips character data and substitutes 0
Characters in C++ are integral types with numeric ASCII values, allowing implicit type promotion to match function parameter types
questions.explanation: In C++, char is an integral type (e.g. 'A' has ASCII value 65), so the arguments ('A' and 5) undergo implicit conversions to match the parameter types int and char.

questions.question: If `int Numbers[20]; int *p;`, why is `p = Numbers;` valid while `Numbers = p;` causes a compilation error?
options: Pointers cannot be assigned to arrays without explicit void* casting
Numbers is stored on the heap, whereas p is stored on the stack
Numbers is a constant pointer representing the array's fixed base address, and constant identifiers cannot be assigned to
p has 20 elements while Numbers has only 1
questions.explanation: An array name is a constant pointer pointing to the array's first element; because it is a constant identifier, it cannot be reassigned.

questions.question: Consider the code: `int *p1 = new int; int *p2 = new int; *p1 = 10; *p2 = 20; *p1 = *p2; *p1 = 30;`. What values are printed by `cout << *p1 << " " << *p2;`?
questions.explanation: The statement *p1 = *p2 copies the integer value 20 into the memory location of p1. Then *p1 = 30 updates only p1's memory, leaving *p2 unchanged at 20.

questions.question: When a file is opened in append access mode (`ios::app`), where is the writing pointer placed and how does writing behave?
options: The writing pointer is automatically placed at the end of the file, and any new data is appended to existing content
The file is cleared to 0 bytes and the pointer starts at byte 0
The writing pointer is locked until seekp() is called
The writing pointer starts at byte 0 and overwrites existing characters
questions.explanation: In append mode (ios::app), the writing pointer is automatically positioned at the end of the file, ensuring all output is appended.

questions.question: What is the primary operational advantage of binary files over text files when storing large amounts of numerical data?
options: Binary files can be opened without using file streams
Binary files eliminate character conversion overhead and store data in compact internal format without line-formatting characters
Binary files can only be accessed sequentially
Binary files are directly human-readable in standard text editors
questions.explanation: Binary files store data in the exact binary format used in RAM, avoiding costly character-to-number conversions and saving disk space.

questions.question: How does calling an object's member function differ syntactically from defining that member function outside the class?
options: Calling uses the dot operator (.) on an object instance, while defining uses the scope resolution operator (::) with the class name
Calling requires the class name, while defining requires only the object identifier
Calling requires the -> operator, while defining requires the * operator
Calling uses the scope resolution operator (::), while defining uses the dot operator (.)
questions.explanation: The dot operator specifies a member of an object instance (e.g. today.output()), while the scope resolution operator connects the class name to the function header (e.g. Year::output()).

questions.question: Why does C++ provide support for constructor overloading in class definitions?
options: To allow private member variables to become publicly accessible
To automatically free memory when an object goes out of scope
To permit objects of the same class to be initialized in different ways according to the arguments supplied
To allow constructors to return error codes of varying types
questions.explanation: Constructor overloading allows a class to have multiple constructors with different parameter lists, enabling flexible object initialization.

questions.question: Why does C++ prohibit assigning one array directly to another using `arr1 = arr2;` even when their data types and dimensions are identical?
options: The assignment operator is reserved exclusively for pointer-to-pointer types
Array identifiers are constant pointers representing fixed memory blocks, and constant identifiers cannot be assigned to
Arrays in C++ can only be copied using recursive procedures
Arrays are allocated in read-only program memory
questions.explanation: An array name is a constant pointer to allocated memory; because constant pointers cannot be reassigned, whole-array assignment is disallowed.

questions.question: If the user enters 'AB', presses Enter, and then enters 'CD', what character value does `c3` hold after `cin.get(c1); cin.get(c2); cin.get(c3);`?
options: '\n' because cin.get() reads every character including the newline character produced by the Enter key
' ' (space) because the buffer replaces newlines with blanks
A null character '\0'
'C' because newline characters are automatically bypassed by cin.get()
questions.explanation: Unlike >>, cin.get() does not skip whitespace or newlines. c1 receives 'A', c2 receives 'B', and c3 receives the newline character '\n'.

questions.question: What happens if a function is called before its definition in a C++ file without any prior function prototype?
options: The linker links the function dynamically at runtime
The call is ignored and returns void
The compiler assumes the function returns an int and compiles with a warning
A compilation error occurs because the function name has not been declared
questions.explanation: In C++, an identifier must be declared before it is referenced; calling a function before defining it without a prototype produces a compilation error.

questions.question: In the recursive implementation `unsigned int factorial(unsigned int n) { return n == 0 ? 1 : n * factorial(n - 1); }`, what is the role of `n == 0 ? 1`?
options: It is an exception handler for invalid unsigned parameters
It is the recursive step that continues function calls
It is the base case condition that terminates recursion and initiates stack unwinding
It is an inline expansion hint for the compiler
questions.explanation: The condition n == 0 is the base case that terminates recursion, returning 1 and allowing previous recursive calls to compute their products.

questions.question: What does the statement `*p++ = *q++;` accomplish in C++?
options: It assigns the address of q to p and increments the dereferenced value
It increments *p and *q before performing the assignment
It causes a compilation syntax error due to conflicting post-increment operators
It assigns the value pointed to by q to the location pointed to by p, and then increments both pointers p and q
questions.explanation: Because post-increment is applied after value evaluation, the value of *q is copied to *p, and then both pointer addresses are incremented by one unit.

questions.question: What is the consequence of failing to check if a pointer returned by `new` is `NULL` before using it in C++?
options: The dynamic allocation is automatically deferred until memory becomes free
If heap memory is exhausted, the pointer is null, and dereferencing it causes undefined behavior or a program crash
The operating system reclaims stack memory to satisfy the allocation
The compiler issues a warning and converts the pointer into a static variable
questions.explanation: If dynamic memory allocation fails, new returns a null pointer; dereferencing a null pointer causes severe runtime faults or system crashes.

questions.question: How does reading data from a binary file using `read()` differ from reading from a text file using `>>`?
options: read() can only be called on character variables, whereas >> works on all types
read() processes formatted ASCII numbers, while >> reads raw unformatted bytes
read() reads an entire contiguous block of bytes directly into memory at once, whereas >> parses individual values separated by whitespace
read() requires the file to be closed after every read operation
questions.explanation: Binary I/O uses read() to transfer an entire record's memory representation at once, whereas text I/O uses >> to read and parse values piece by piece.

questions.question: What occurs when a C++ program attempts to open a non-existent file for reading using `ios::in`?
options: The open operation fails, the stream object evaluates to null/zero, and fail() returns true
The stream waits until another program creates the file
C++ automatically creates an empty file on disk
The file pointer is initialized at ios::end
questions.explanation: A file opened for reading must already exist; if it does not, open() fails to create a valid stream object and fail() returns true.

questions.question: What is the specific visibility rule for class members declared under the `protected` access specifier?
options: They are accessible only to global functions
They are accessible to all functions in the program
They are accessible only to member functions of the class and to classes derived from that class
They can only be accessed from within constructors
questions.explanation: Protected members cannot be accessed by external code, but remain accessible to methods of the class itself and to derived subclasses.

questions.question: In C++, why is a constructor definition prohibited from specifying any return type, not even `void`?
options: Because constructors are called automatically upon object creation to initialize state and by language design cannot return values
Because constructors must always return an integer status code to the operating system
Because constructors are only executed during compile-time optimization
Because specifying a return type converts the constructor into a destructor
questions.explanation: Constructors are dedicated to object initialization upon declaration; language semantics forbid specifying any return type, including void.
